steps.h: Pick the seat, and check you can hold it
steps.p: Each office has its own rules: how old you must be, how long you must have lived there, whether you must be registered to vote there. The state's candidate page lists them.

steps.h: Find the office you file with
steps.p: Seats in Congress, statewide and in the legislature are usually filed with the state. A county, city, school or district seat is usually filed with your county elections office or your city or town clerk. Call them and ask which forms you need: that question is their job.

steps.h: Put the filing dates in your calendar
steps.p: You can only file during a short window, often months before the election. Miss it and the seat waits for the election after. The state sets the dates for each election.

steps.h: Get your name on the paper
steps.p: Most places ask for a declaration of candidacy and either a filing fee or voters' signatures. Signatures are checked one by one and the ones that fail are struck off, so collect well over the minimum.

steps.h: Set up the money side before you spend
steps.p: Many states want a campaign committee, a treasurer and a separate bank account, registered with the state, before you raise or spend a dollar. The office that keeps campaign money reports says what yours needs.

steps.h: File, then go and meet people
steps.p: File the way your state asks, in person if it says so, and keep the receipt. Then knock on doors. Nobody ran against the winner last time, so you may be the first person ever to ask these neighbours for their vote.
Nobody wins alone. Start a gathering for this seat: a time and a place where the people who want it filled can meet and back a candidate.

training.name: The Local Government Playbook
training.what: A free online course for local elected officials and candidates: strategies for governing and for working with your community.
training.free: The course page marks it Free (a paid coaching offer sits beside it; it is not needed).

training.name: Ballot access in your state (Ballotpedia)
training.what: Signatures, fees and filing deadlines for state and federal offices, office by office, each with its source.

training.name: Your state's league of cities and towns
training.what: The association of your state's cities and towns. New council members learn the job here.
training.free: Its website is free to read; what each league offers differs.

training.name: Your state's association of counties
training.what: The association of your state's counties and county officials.
training.free: Its website is free to read; what each association offers differs.

training.name: Newly Elected Leaders Toolkit (ICMA)
training.what: For after you win: what the job is, and the rules on open meetings and public records. A free download from the association of city and county managers.

training.name: My Congressional District (US Census Bureau)
training.what: The people, jobs and homes in any congressional district, from the Census. Know who you want to serve.

training.name: Campaign Guide for Congressional Candidates (FEC)
training.what: Only if you run for Congress: the federal rules on raising, spending and reporting campaign money.
training.free: A free PDF from the Federal Election Commission.

training.name: The FEC's videos
training.what: Only if you run for Congress: short videos on the federal money rules, from the commission that enforces them.

finders.name: Your local League of Women Voters
finders.what: The League's own finder for its local leagues. Search by ZIP.

finders.name: Rotary clubs near you
finders.what: Rotary's own finder for its local clubs.

finders.name: Political committees in your state (FEC)
finders.what: Every committee registered with the FEC with an address in your state, PACs included.

finders.name: State and local committees
finders.what: Local PACs and candidate committees report to the state, not the FEC. The FEC's directory names the office that keeps those reports in your state, with its address.
